messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 20
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: African
  relationship_status: Single
  occupation: Doctor
  trauma_type: Combat
  pcl5: 63

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Somatic (Breathlessness): Difficulty breathing or feeling short of breath, Auditory (Silence): Sudden or complete silence, Violence: Violence
  Memory: Blocked Before Complete: I find myself pushing the memory away before I can fully recall it, Fragmented Pieces: My memories of the event come in disconnected pieces that do not fit together, Memory Gaps: There are parts of the event that I simply cannot remember no matter how hard I try
  Negative Appraisals: Identity Loss: I feel like I don't know myself anymore, Shattered Beliefs: My beliefs about how the world works have been completely destroyed, Hypervigilance: I have to be on guard all the time

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Triggers
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Triggers

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

# Clinical Vignette: Kwame

Kwame was twenty years old when he deployed with his medical unit to a conflict zone in West Africa. He had joined the armed forces partly out of a sense of duty to his heritage, partly because a career in medicine felt more attainable through military sponsorship than through the civilian route his family had assumed he would take. He was competent, focused, and by all accounts well-liked by his unit. The first weeks were procedural—setting up field hospitals, triaging minor injuries, learning the rhythms of a place where violence was abstract until it became concrete. Then came the morning when a transport convoy was ambushed not far from the medical facility where Kwame was stationed. The casualties arrived in waves. He remembers the noise—the rotor blades of the helicopter, the shouting, the metallic clang of instruments. He remembers the blood, the smell of it, the weight of a soldier's arm across his shoulders as Kwame tried to stabilize a pneumothorax. What he does not remember—what his mind refuses to hold—is what happened in the hour after that. There are fragments: a sudden, absolute silence when the generator failed; the face of a young man on the operating table; his own hands shaking so badly he had to step back. But the pieces do not connect. When he tries to reconstruct it, his mind slides away, as though the memory itself is too heavy to hold, and he finds himself pushing the recollection aside before it can fully form.

Kwame returned home after eight months. The homecoming was quiet. His family was relieved, proud, cautious—they could see something had shifted in him, though he could not yet articulate what. For the first month, he managed. He enrolled in his pre-medical coursework at the university and tried to resume the life he had imagined. But the world felt fundamentally different now, and so did he. He had come to believe that he no longer knew who he was—the person who had wanted to be a doctor, who had believed in order and healing and the basic decency of people, that person seemed to have been left behind in that field hospital. His beliefs about how the world worked had been shattered. He had seen what humans were capable of doing to each other, had felt the weight of his own helplessness, and no amount of intellectual reframing seemed to restore the naive certainty he once possessed. He had to be on guard all the time now; the world was not safe, and neither was he. This constant vigilance exhausted him, but it also felt necessary, a kind of armor against a reality he could no longer deny.

The triggers came unpredictably, each one pulling him back into a state of acute threat. Sudden silence—the kind that falls in a lecture hall when the air conditioning cuts out, or in the university library when a group of students stops talking—would send his heart racing. His breath would become shallow and difficult, as though his chest had tightened around his lungs. In those moments, the fragmentation of his memory became almost unbearable. The silence seemed to unlock something, and pieces of that missing hour would surface without warning: an image of blood pooling on a surgical drape, the sensation of someone gripping his wrist, a voice calling out a name he could not quite place. These fragments arrived disconnected and terrifying, and they reinforced his conviction that he was fundamentally broken, that whatever had happened in that silence had unmade him in ways he could not repair. Violence—even in films or in news reports—triggered the same cycle: his breathing would become labored, his mind would splinter, and the conviction that he could no longer trust his own judgment or his ability to protect himself would deepen. Each trigger seemed to confirm what the fragmented memories whispered: that he was not safe, that the world was not safe, and that there was no going back.

By the time Kwame sought help, he had withdrawn from his coursework. He was still living at home, still telling his parents he was "managing," but he had stopped going to campus. The thought of being in a crowded classroom, of the unexpected sounds and movements, of the possibility that silence might fall and leave him exposed to his own fractured recollections, felt impossible to bear. He was afraid that if he allowed himself to remember, he would discover that the person he had been was truly gone. What he wanted most, he told his therapist in their first session, was to feel like himself again—but he was no longer certain such a person existed.
